A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TARO research, and all supplied pages support comparison through readable text, equations, tables, and rendered figures. v1 ends after the references; v2 includes Supplementary Material A-F. Supplementary additions are assessed as newly documented content, without assuming the experiments were newly performed.

before.justification: v1 reports original VGGSound and Landscape evaluations, subjective audio ratings, component ablations, and qualitative comparisons in Tables 1-6 and Figures 5-6.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and includes additional ablation metrics, temporal-feature comparisons, training-progress results, and qualitative examples in its supplement.

M1.justification: The flow-based transformer, onset conditioning through AdaLN, timestep-weighted alignment loss, convolutional projection, and inference procedure remain unchanged. Added explanations of conditioning overhead and frozen modules clarify the existing design; they do not establish a changed method.

E1.justification: Both versions train and evaluate on VGGSound and perform zero-shot evaluation on Landscape for video-to-audio synthesis. The supplementary comparisons and examples remain within this coverage. Removing the prose list of Landscape categories does not establish removal of those categories from evaluation.

E2.justification: The seven external baselines in Tables 1-2 remain unchanged. Supplementary Table 11 newly compares onset cues against energy-control and down-sampled-mel conditioning variants, providing a limited expansion of evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: The original splits, preprocessing, training budget, model configuration, and sampling settings remain unchanged. New supplementary evaluations introduce training-checkpoint comparisons and ImageBind, onset-related, and temporal-offset metrics. Table 11 specifies equal 500k-iteration training for its feature variants. Table 12 ambiguously repeats 'Onset Acc' where the accompanying prose names both Onset Acc and Onset AP.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the supporting analyses: Table 11 tests alternative temporal conditioning signals, Figure 7 compares training progress with and without TRA, and Figures 8-10 add six qualitative cases. Tables 7-10 also expand the existing component, projection, encoder, and injection-depth ablations with FID, IS, and KL results.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same MOS results with 95% confidence intervals in Table 1 and describe that uncertainty practice in Section 5.1. Neither reports additional training seeds, repeated-run uncertainty, or significance tests. The newly disclosed participant and clip counts describe the existing user study rather than a changed uncertainty procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 1-6 retain their numerical results, but the supplement substantially expands reported outcomes. Tables 7-10 add metrics for existing ablations; Table 11 reports onset-cue versus energy-control alignment accuracy of 97.19% versus 96.10%; Table 12 adds TARO's ImageBind score of 64.22 and temporal offset of 0.97 seconds. Figure 7 adds lower-FAD training trajectories with TRA, and Figures 8-10 add qualitative findings. These are added results, not improvements over v1's retained scores.

T1.justification: Equations 1-9 retain the same flow formulation, objectives, AdaLN expressions, alignment weighting, and projection relationship. The supplement introduces no new formal assumptions, mathematical definitions, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: v2 removes the introduction's claim to be the first work applying representation alignment to video-to-audio synthesis, narrowing its priority claim. The two central contributions and the abstract's reported fidelity and synchronization advantages remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Unlike v1, Supplementary Section E explicitly identifies limitations involving training-data scale, fixed video length, human speech, and dependence on onset-prediction accuracy. Sections C-D add interpretations of metric tradeoffs and training progress, while Section 4.2 adds a computational rationale for AdaLN conditioning. These substantially expand the discussion of mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability statement and project-page access information. Supplementary Section B discloses that the existing MOS study used 20 VGGSound videos, 10 Landscape videos, and 20 participants aged 24-30, with specific rating instructions and randomized ordering within video groups. These improve documentation without establishing a changed study.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused discussion of TiVA and ReWaS temporal conditioning and citations to DDIM, DNI, FRAG, and TPC, while shortening the flow-model survey and removing the first-use alignment claim. The overall positioning remains similar. TiVA/ReWaS feature attributions are internally reversed between Section 2 and Supplementary Section D.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites expand TRA/OAC motivation, shorten related-work and dataset descriptions, and make supplementary cross-references specific. The added material is organized into Sections A-F, but the main section order and most method, results, and conclusion prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 3 into a more compact arrangement and substantially expands the visual presentation. Tables 7-10 redisplay existing ablations with additional metric columns; Tables 11-12 add comparisons; Figure 7 adds a training curve; and Figures 8-10 provide six additional qualitative examples. The original main benchmark displays are largely retained.

improvement.justification: The supplementary controls, training-progress evidence, user-study details, and concrete limitations improve support and transparency around the unchanged core results. These gains are tempered by reporting errors: reversed TiVA/ReWaS feature attributions, duplicated onset-metric headings in Table 12, and the claim that depth 2 has the highest IS although Table 10 gives 56.57 at depth 2 versus 56.60 at depth 4.
